summary:
SymbioN is a soil-recovery decision tool that turns NASA Earth observation data into a practical farming plan. We developed a Python engine, built on Google Colab, that reads NASA SMAP soil moisture and ECOSTRESS land surface temperature data, detects drought and heat stress, and recommends a symbiotic crop rotation: legumes and cover crops that fix nitrogen naturally and support soil health. We also designed an app prototype that shows farmers a clear alert and a ready recommendation.

This addresses the Field Shift challenge by helping farms adapt to heat and drought in regions like Jazan. Instead of reacting after crops are damaged, farmers get an early warning and know what to plant next to help the soil recover.

It matters because one third of the world’s soil is degraded. SymbioN supports soil health, reduces the need for chemical fertilizer, and relies on open NASA data. Our demo values are simulated; next, we will connect live data and calibrate with field tests.

Project Details (English)

SymbioN: turning NASA soil data into a plan that helps stressed soil recover

SymbioN is a decision tool for farmers facing heat and drought. A Python engine reads soil moisture from NASA SMAP and land surface temperature from NASA ECOSTRESS, compares them with stress thresholds (root-zone moisture below 20% and surface temperature above 35 °C), and classifies the stress level of a field. It then produces three outputs: an early alert, a “soil fingerprint” that summarizes the soil’s condition, and a symbiotic crop rotation plan, for example faba beans in winter and cowpeas in summer, which tolerate heat. The farmer receives a ready decision instead of raw numbers.

We built it in Python (with pandas) on Google Colab, using NASA Earthdata products in HDF5 format: SMAP L4, SMAP L2 (L2_SM_P_E) and ECOSTRESS. We also designed an app mock-up to show how a farmer would see the alert and the recommendation. No special hardware is needed, since everything runs on free cloud tools and a standard computer.

The benefits are practical. Farmers get an early warning before the crop suffers, and a natural plan based on legumes and cover crops that fix nitrogen, improve soil structure and support soil life. This reduces the need for chemical fertilizer and its cost. The intended impact is healthier soil for farmers in Jazan and other arid regions, and clearer information for agricultural planners. Because NASA data is open and global, the approach can scale to other regions.

The creative aspect is that most tools predict crop yield, while SymbioN treats the soil itself, using stress signals from space to trigger a natural rotation plan.

Our team considered several factors. SMAP gives a regional picture at about 9 km, so we combine it with ECOSTRESS at about 70 m for field-level detail. Our demo values are simulated and our thresholds are preliminary and adjustable, and we state this openly. We chose a rule-based logic so farmers can understand why a crop is recommended, and we considered Jazan’s heat and seasons. Next, we will connect live NASA data, calibrate the system with laboratory tests and ground sensors, and add more crops and regions.

1. NASA SMAP Mission (Products: SMAP L4_SM for root-zone soil moisture & SMAP L2_SM_A/P for high-resolution soil moisture telemetry).

2. NASA ECOSTRESS Mission on the ISS (Product: Land Surface Temperature and thermal stress monitoring).

3. FAO (Food and Agriculture Organization) – Global Soil Partnership (إحصائية تدهور 33% من أتربة العالم).

4. Google Colab, Python (pandas), and NASA Earthdata HDF5 processing framework.
